segs.e: Linked Discourses 3.1
1. Shackles
Young
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “bhavampi no gotamo anuttaraṁ sammāsambodhiṁ abhisambuddhoti paṭijānātī”ti?
segs.e: “Does the worthy Gotama claim to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening?”

segs.p: “Yañhi taṁ, mahārāja, sammā vadamāno vadeyya ‘anuttaraṁ sammāsambodhiṁ abhisambuddho’ti, mameva taṁ sammā vadamāno vadeyya.
segs.e: “If anyone should rightly be said to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening, it’s me.
For, Great King, I have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening.”

segs.p: “Yepi te, bho gotama, samaṇabrāhmaṇā saṅghino gaṇino gaṇācariyā ñātā yasassino titthakarā sādhusammatā bahujanassa, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: “Well, there are those ascetics and brahmins who lead an order and a community, and tutor a community. They’re well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people. That is,

segs.p: pūraṇo kassapo, makkhali gosālo, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto, sañcayo belaṭṭhaputto, pakudho kaccāyano, ajito kesakambalo;
segs.e: Pūraṇa Kassapa, the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita of the hair blanket.

segs.p: tepi mayā ‘anuttaraṁ sammāsambodhiṁ abhisambuddhoti paṭijānāthā’ti puṭṭhā samānā anuttaraṁ sammāsambodhiṁ abhisambuddhoti na paṭijānanti.
segs.e: I also asked them whether they claimed to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening, but they made no such claim.

segs.p: Kiṁ pana bhavaṁ gotamo daharo ceva jātiyā navo ca pabbajjāyā”ti?
segs.e: So why do you, given that you’re so young in age and newly gone forth?”

segs.p: “Cattāro kho me, mahārāja, daharāti na uññātabbā, daharāti na paribhotabbā.
segs.e: “Great king, these four things should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young.
What four?

segs.p: Khattiyo kho, mahārāja, daharoti na uññātabbo, daharoti na paribhotabbo.
segs.e: An aristocrat,

segs.p: Urago kho, mahārāja, daharoti na uññātabbo, daharoti na paribhotabbo.
segs.e: a serpent,

segs.p: Aggi kho, mahārāja, daharoti na uññātabbo, daharoti na paribhotabbo.
segs.e: a fire,

segs.p: Bhikkhu, kho, mahārāja, daharoti na uññātabbo, daharoti na paribhotabbo.
segs.e: and a mendicant.

segs.p: Ime kho, mahārāja, cattāro daharāti na uññātabbā, daharāti na paribhotabbā”ti.
segs.e: These four things should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“A man should not despise
an aristocrat of impeccable lineage,
high-born and famous,
just because they’re young.
For it’s possible that that lord of mankind,
as aristocrat, will gain the throne.
And in his anger he’ll execute a royal punishment,
and have you violently beaten.
Hence you should avoid him
for the sake of your own life.
Whether in village or wilderness,
wherever a serpent is seen,
a man should not look down on it
or despise it for its youth.
With its rainbow of colors,
the serpent of fiery breath glides along.
It lashes out and bites the fool,
both men and women alike.
Hence you should avoid it
for the sake of your own life.
A fire devours a vast amount,
a conflagration with a blackened trail.
A man should not look down on it
just because it’s young.
For once it gets fuel
it’ll become a big conflagration.
It’ll lash out and burn the fool,
both men and women alike.
Hence you should avoid it
for the sake of your own life.
When a forest is burned by fire,
a conflagration with a blackened trail,
the shoots will spring up there again,
with the passing of the days and nights.
But if a mendicant endowed with ethics
burns you with their power,
you’ll have no children or livestock,
nor will your heirs find wealth.
Childless and heirless you become,
like a palm-tree stump.
That’s why an astute person,
seeing what’s good for themselves,
would always treat these properly:
a serpent, a conflagration,
a famous aristocrat,
and a mendicant endowed with ethics.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Buddha,
“Excellent, sir! Excellent!

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṁ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṁ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṁ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṁ dhāreyya: ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṁ bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito.
segs.e: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

segs.p: Esāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavantaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca.
segs.e: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

segs.p: Upāsakaṁ maṁ, bhante, bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṁ saraṇaṁ gatan”ti.
segs.e: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
Linked Discourses 3.2
1. Shackles
A Person
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “kati nu kho, bhante, purisassa dhammā ajjhattaṁ uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāyā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how many things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort?”

segs.p: “Tayo kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammā ajjhattaṁ uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya.
segs.e: “Great king, three things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.
What three?

segs.p: Lobho kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammo ajjhattaṁ uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya.
segs.e: Greed,

segs.p: Doso kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammo ajjhattaṁ uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya.
segs.e: hate,

segs.p: Moho kho, mahārāja, purisassa dhammo ajjhattaṁ uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya.
segs.e: and delusion.

segs.p: Ime kho, mahārāja, tayo purisassa dhammā ajjhattaṁ uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāyā”ti.
segs.e: These three things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“When greed, hate, and delusion,
originate inside oneself,
they harm a person of wicked heart,
as a bamboo is destroyed by its own fruit.”
Linked Discourses 3.3
1. Shackles
Old Age and Death
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “atthi nu kho, bhante, jātassa aññatra jarāmaraṇā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, for someone who has been reborn, is there any exemption from old age and death?”
“Great king, for someone who has been reborn, there’s no exemption from old age and death.

segs.p: Yepi te, mahārāja, khattiyamahāsālā aḍḍhā mahaddhanā mahābhogā pahūtajātarūparajatā pahūtavittūpakaraṇā pahūtadhanadhaññā, tesampi jātānaṁ natthi aññatra jarāmaraṇā.
segs.e: Even for well-to-do aristocrats,
brahmins,

segs.p: gahapatimahāsālā aḍḍhā mahaddhanā mahābhogā pahūtajātarūparajatā pahūtavittūpakaraṇā pahūtadhanadhaññā, tesampi jātānaṁ natthi aññatra jarāmaraṇā.
segs.e: or householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain—when they’re born, there’s no exemption from old age and death.

segs.p: Yepi te, mahārāja, bhikkhū arahanto khīṇāsavā vusitavanto katakaraṇīyā ohitabhārā anuppattasadatthā parikkhīṇabhavasaṁyojanā sammadaññāvimuttā, tesampāyaṁ kāyo bhedanadhammo nikkhepanadhammo”ti.
segs.e: Even for mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—their bodies are liable to break up and be laid to rest.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“Fancy chariots of kings wear out,
and even this body gets old.
But the truth of the good never gets old—
so the good proclaim to the good.”
Linked Discourses 3.4
1. Shackles
Loved
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

segs.p: ‘kesaṁ nu kho piyo attā, kesaṁ appiyo attā’ti?
segs.e: ‘Who are those who love themselves? And who are those who don’t love themselves?’
Then it occurred to me:

segs.p: ‘ye ca kho keci kāyena duccaritaṁ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṁ caranti, manasā duccaritaṁ caranti;
segs.e: ‘Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind
don’t love themselves.
Even though they may say:

segs.p: “piyo no attā”ti, atha kho tesaṁ appiyo attā’.
segs.e: “I love myself”, they don’t really.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yañhi appiyo appiyassa kareyya, taṁ te attanāva attano karonti;
segs.e: It’s because they treat themselves like an enemy.
That’s why they don’t love themselves.

segs.p: Ye ca kho keci kāyena sucaritaṁ caranti, vācāya sucaritaṁ caranti, manasā sucaritaṁ caranti;
segs.e: Those who do good things by way of body, speech, and mind
do love themselves.
Even though they may say:

segs.p: ‘appiyo no attā’ti; atha kho tesaṁ piyo attā.
segs.e: “I don’t love myself”, they do really.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yañhi piyo piyassa kareyya, taṁ te attanāva attano karonti;
segs.e: It’s because they treat themselves like a loved one.
That’s why they do love themselves.’”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

segs.p: Ye hi keci, mahārāja, kāyena duccaritaṁ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṁ caranti, manasā duccaritaṁ caranti;
‘piyo no attā’ti, atha kho tesaṁ appiyo attā.
Yañhi, mahārāja, appiyo appiyassa kareyya, taṁ te attanāva attano karonti;
Ye ca kho keci, mahārāja, kāyena sucaritaṁ caranti, vācāya sucaritaṁ caranti, manasā sucaritaṁ caranti;
Yañhi, mahārāja, piyo piyassa kareyya, taṁ te attanāva attano karonti;

segs.e: “If you knew your self as beloved,
you’d not yoke yourself to wickedness.
For happiness is not easy to find
by someone who does bad deeds.
When you’re seized by the terminator
as you give up your human life,
what can you call your own?
What do you take when you go?
What goes with you,
like a shadow that never leaves?
Both the good and the bad
that a mortal does in this life
is what they can call their own.
That’s what they take when they go.
That’s what goes with them,
like a shadow that never leaves.
That’s why you should do good,
investing in the future life.
The good deeds of sentient beings
support them in the next world.”
Linked Discourses 3.5
1. Shackles
Self-Protected
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

segs.p: ‘kesaṁ nu kho rakkhito attā, kesaṁ arakkhito attā’ti?
segs.e: ‘Who are those who protect themselves? And who are those who don’t protect themselves?’
Then it occurred to me:

segs.p: ‘ye kho keci kāyena duccaritaṁ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṁ caranti, manasā duccaritaṁ caranti;
segs.e: ‘Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind
don’t protect themselves.

segs.p: Kiñcāpi te hatthikāyo vā rakkheyya, assakāyo vā rakkheyya, rathakāyo vā rakkheyya, pattikāyo vā rakkheyya;
segs.e: Even if they’re protected by a company of elephants, cavalry, chariots, or infantry,
they still don’t protect themselves.
Why is that?

segs.p: Bāhirā hesā rakkhā, nesā rakkhā ajjhattikā;
segs.e: Because such protection is exterior, not interior.
That’s why they don’t protect themselves.

segs.p: Ye ca kho keci kāyena sucaritaṁ caranti, vācāya sucaritaṁ caranti, manasā sucaritaṁ caranti;
segs.e: Those who do good things by way of body, speech, and mind
do protect themselves.

segs.p: Kiñcāpi te neva hatthikāyo rakkheyya, na assakāyo rakkheyya, na rathakāyo rakkheyya, na pattikāyo rakkheyya;
segs.e: Even if they’re not protected by a company of elephants, cavalry, chariots, or infantry,
they still protect themselves.
Why is that?

segs.p: Ajjhattikā hesā rakkhā, nesā rakkhā bāhirā;
segs.e: Because such protection is interior, not exterior.
That’s why they do protect themselves.’”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

segs.p: Ye hi keci, mahārāja, kāyena duccaritaṁ caranti …pe…
Bāhirā hesā, mahārāja, rakkhā, nesā rakkhā ajjhattikā;
Ye hi keci, mahārāja, kāyena sucaritaṁ caranti, vācāya sucaritaṁ caranti, manasā sucaritaṁ caranti;
Kiñcāpi te neva hatthikāyo rakkheyya, na assakāyo rakkheyya, na rathakāyo rakkheyya, na pattikāyo rakkheyya;
Ajjhattikā hesā, mahārāja, rakkhā, nesā rakkhā bāhirā;

segs.e: “Restraint of the body is good;
restraint of speech is good;
restraint of mind is good;
everywhere, restraint is good.
A sincere person, restrained everywhere,
is said to be ‘protected’.”
Linked Discourses 3.6
1. Shackles
Few
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

segs.p: ‘appakā te sattā lokasmiṁ ye uḷāre uḷāre bhoge labhitvā na ceva majjanti, na ca pamajjanti, na ca kāmesu gedhaṁ āpajjanti, na ca sattesu vippaṭipajjanti.
segs.e: ‘Few are the sentient beings in the world who, when they obtain luxury possessions, don’t grow indulgent and negligent, giving in to greed for sensual pleasures, and doing the wrong thing by others.

segs.p: Atha kho eteva bahutarā sattā lokasmiṁ ye uḷāre uḷāre bhoge labhitvā majjanti ceva pamajjanti ca kāmesu ca gedhaṁ āpajjanti, sattesu ca vippaṭipajjantī’”ti.
segs.e: There are many more who, when they obtain luxury possessions, do grow indulgent and negligent, giving in to greed for sensual pleasures, and doing the wrong thing by others.’”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

segs.p: Appakā te, mahārāja, sattā lokasmiṁ, ye uḷāre uḷāre bhoge labhitvā na ceva majjanti, na ca pamajjanti, na ca kāmesu gedhaṁ āpajjanti, na ca sattesu vippaṭipajjanti.
Atha kho eteva bahutarā sattā lokasmiṁ, ye uḷāre uḷāre bhoge labhitvā majjanti ceva pamajjanti ca kāmesu ca gedhaṁ āpajjanti, sattesu ca vippaṭipajjantī”ti.

segs.e: “Full of desire for possessions and pleasures,
greedy, infatuated by sensual pleasures;
they don’t notice that they’ve gone too far,
like deer ensnared in a trap set out.
It’ll be bitter later on;
for the result will be bad for them.”
Linked Discourses 3.7
1. Shackles
Judgment
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “idhāhaṁ, bhante, aḍḍakaraṇe nisinno passāmi khattiyamahāsālepi brāhmaṇamahāsālepi gahapatimahāsālepi aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate pahūtavittūpakaraṇe pahūtadhanadhaññe kāmahetu kāmanidānaṁ kāmādhikaraṇaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsante.
segs.e: “Sir, when I’m sitting in court I see well-to-do aristocrats, brahmins, and householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain. But they tell deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures.
Then it occurred to me:

segs.p: ‘alaṁ dāni me aḍḍakaraṇena, bhadramukho dāni aḍḍakaraṇena paññāyissatī’”ti.
segs.e: ‘Enough with passing judgment today. Now my dearest will be known by the judgments he makes.’”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!

segs.p: Yepi te, mahārāja, khattiyamahāsālā brāhmaṇamahāsālā gahapatimahāsālā aḍḍhā mahaddhanā mahābhogā pahūtajātarūparajatā pahūtavittūpakaraṇā pahūtadhanadhaññā kāmahetu kāmanidānaṁ kāmādhikaraṇaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsanti;
segs.e: Those who are well-to-do aristocrats, brahmins, and householders tell deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures.

segs.p: tesaṁ taṁ bhavissati dīgharattaṁ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.
segs.e: That is for their lasting harm and suffering.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“Full of desire for possessions and pleasures,
greedy, infatuated by sensual pleasures;
they don’t notice that they’ve gone too far,
like fish swiftly snared.
It’ll be bitter later on;
for the result will be bad for them.”
Linked Discourses 3.8
1. Shackles
With Queen Mallikā
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo mallikāya deviyā saddhiṁ uparipāsādavaragato hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala was upstairs in the royal longhouse together with Queen Mallikā.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the king said to the queen,

segs.p: “atthi nu kho te, mallike, kocañño attanā piyataro”ti?
segs.e: “Mallikā, is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

segs.p: “Natthi kho me, mahārāja, kocañño attanā piyataro.
segs.e: “No, Great King, there isn’t.

segs.p: Tuyhaṁ pana, mahārāja, atthañño koci attanā piyataro”ti?
segs.e: But is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

segs.p: “Mayhampi kho, mallike, natthañño koci attanā piyataro”ti.
segs.e: “For me also, Mallikā, there’s no one.”

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo pāsādā orohitvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala came downstairs from the stilt longhouse, went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “idhāhaṁ, bhante, mallikāya deviyā saddhiṁ uparipāsādavaragato mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavocaṁ:
‘atthi nu kho te, mallike, kocañño attanā piyataro’ti?
Evaṁ vutte, bhante, mallikā devī maṁ etadavoca:
‘natthi kho me, mahārāja, kocañño attanā piyataro.
Tuyhaṁ pana, mahārāja, atthañño koci attanā piyataro’ti?
Evaṁ vuttāhaṁ, bhante, mallikaṁ deviṁ etadavocaṁ:
‘mayhampi kho, mallike, natthañño koci attanā piyataro’”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha spoke this verse:
“Having explored every quarter with the mind,
one finds no one dearer than oneself.
Likewise for others, each holds themselves dear;
so one who desires self-knowledge <j>would harm no other.”
Linked Discourses 3.9
1. Shackles
Sacrifice
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena rañño pasenadissa kosalassa mahāyañño paccupaṭṭhito hoti, pañca ca usabhasatāni pañca ca vacchatarasatāni pañca ca vacchatarisatāni pañca ca ajasatāni pañca ca urabbhasatāni thūṇūpanītāni honti yaññatthāya.
segs.e: Now at that time a grand sacrifice had been set up for King Pasenadi of Kosala. Bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats and rams—five hundred of each—had been led to the pillar for the sacrifice.

segs.p: Yepissa te honti dāsāti vā pessāti vā kammakarāti vā, tepi daṇḍatajjitā bhayatajjitā assumukhā rudamānā parikammāni karonti.
segs.e: His bondservants, servants, and workers did their jobs under threat of punishment and danger, weeping with tearful faces.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṁ piṇḍāya pavisiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

segs.p: Sāvatthiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

segs.p: “idha, bhante, rañño pasenadissa kosalassa mahāyañño paccupaṭṭhito hoti, pañca ca usabhasatāni pañca ca vacchatarasatāni pañca ca vacchatarisatāni pañca ca ajasatāni pañca ca urabbhasatāni thūṇūpanītāni honti yaññatthāya.
Yepissa te honti dāsāti vā pessāti vā kammakarāti vā, tepi daṇḍatajjitā bhayatajjitā assumukhā rudamānā parikammāni karontī”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:
“Horse sacrifice, human sacrifice,
the ‘casting of the yoke-pin’, <j>the ‘royal soma drinking’,
and the ‘unimpeded’—
these grand, violent sacrifices yield no great fruit.
The great sages of right comportment
don’t attend sacrifices
where goats, sheep, and cattle
and various creatures are killed.
But the great sages of right comportment
do attend those sacrifices
that are non-violent and propitious,
where goats, sheep, and cattle,
and various creatures are not killed.
An intelligent person should sacrifice like this,
for this sacrifice is very fruitful.
For a sponsor of sacrifices like this,
things get better, not worse.
Such a sacrifice is truly abundant,
and even the deities are pleased.”
Linked Discourses 3.10
1. Shackles
Shackles

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena raññā pasenadinā kosalena mahājanakāyo bandhāpito hoti, appekacce rajjūhi appekacce andūhi appekacce saṅkhalikāhi.
segs.e: Now at that time a large group of people had been put in shackles by King Pasenadi of Kosala—some in ropes, some in manacles, some in chains.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṁ piṇḍāya pavisiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

segs.p: Sāvatthiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

segs.p: “idha, bhante, raññā pasenadinā kosalena mahājanakāyo bandhāpito, appekacce rajjūhi appekacce andūhi appekacce saṅkhalikāhī”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:
“The attentive say that shackle is not strong
that’s made of iron, wood, or knots.
But obsession with jeweled earrings,
concern for your partners and children:
this, say the attentive, is a strong shackle
dragging the indulgent down, hard to escape.
Having cut this one too they go forth,
unconcerned, having given up sensual pleasures.”
Linked Discourses 3.11
2. Childless
Seven Matted-Hair Ascetics

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito bahidvārakoṭṭhake nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and sat outside the gate.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena satta ca jaṭilā satta ca nigaṇṭhā satta ca acelakā satta ca ekasāṭakā satta ca paribbājakā parūḷhakacchanakhalomā khārivividhamādāya bhagavato avidūre atikkamanti.
segs.e: Now at that time seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain ascetics, seven naked ascetics, seven one-cloth ascetics, and seven wanderers passed by not far from the Buddha. Their armpits and bodies were hairy, and their nails were long; and they carried their pack with shoulder-poles.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalaṁ pathaviyaṁ nihantvā yena te satta ca jaṭilā satta ca nigaṇṭhā satta ca acelakā satta ca ekasāṭakā satta ca paribbājakā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā tikkhattuṁ nāmaṁ sāvesi:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi got up from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his joined palms toward those various ascetics, and pronounced his name three times:
“Sirs, I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala! …
I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!”

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo acirapakkantesu tesu sattasu ca jaṭilesu sattasu ca nigaṇṭhesu sattasu ca acelakesu sattasu ca ekasāṭakesu sattasu ca paribbājakesu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then, not long after those ascetics had left, King Pasenadi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “ye te, bhante, loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṁ vā samāpannā ete tesaṁ aññatarā”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, these are among those in the world who are perfected or who are on the path to perfection!”

segs.p: “Dujjānaṁ kho etaṁ, mahārāja, tayā gihinā kāmabhoginā puttasambādhasayanaṁ ajjhāvasantena kāsikacandanaṁ paccanubhontena mālāgandhavilepanaṁ dhārayantena jātarūparajataṁ sādiyantena: ‘ime vā arahanto, ime vā arahattamaggaṁ samāpannā’ti.
segs.e: “Great king, as a layman enjoying sensual pleasures, living at home with your children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency, it’s hard for you to know who is perfected or on the path to perfection.

segs.p: Saṁvāsena kho, mahārāja, sīlaṁ veditabbaṁ. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
segs.e: You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

segs.p: Saṁvohārena kho, mahārāja, soceyyaṁ veditabbaṁ. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
segs.e: You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …

segs.p: Āpadāsu kho, mahārāja, thāmo veditabbo. So ca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
segs.e: You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …

segs.p: Sākacchāya, kho, mahārāja, paññā veditabbā. Sā ca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññenā”ti.
segs.e: You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.”
“It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing,
how well said this was by the Buddha. …

segs.p: ‘dujjānaṁ kho etaṁ, mahārāja, tayā gihinā kāmabhoginā puttasambādhasayanaṁ ajjhāvasantena kāsikacandanaṁ paccanubhontena mālāgandhavilepanaṁ dhārayantena jātarūparajataṁ sādiyantena:
“ime vā arahanto, ime vā arahattamaggaṁ samāpannā”ti.
Saṁvāsena kho, mahārāja, sīlaṁ veditabbaṁ. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
Saṁvohārena kho, mahārāja, soceyyaṁ veditabbaṁ. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
Āpadāsu kho, mahārāja, thāmo veditabbo. So ca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññena.
Sākacchāya kho, mahārāja, paññā veditabbā. Sā ca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaraṁ; manasikarotā, no amanasikarotā; paññavatā, no duppaññenā’ti.
Ete, bhante, mama purisā carā ocarakā janapadaṁ ocaritvā āgacchanti.
segs.e: Sir, these are my spies, my undercover agents returning after spying on the country.

segs.p: Tehi paṭhamaṁ ociṇṇaṁ ahaṁ pacchā osāpayissāmi.
segs.e: I shall later make use of what they first spied out.

segs.p: Idāni te, bhante, taṁ rajojallaṁ pavāhetvā sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū odātavatthā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricāressantī”ti.
segs.e: Now—when they have rinsed off the dust and dirt, and are nicely bathed and anointed, with hair and beard dressed, and dressed in white—they will amuse themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:
“It’s not easy to know a man by his appearance.
You shouldn’t trust them at first sight.
For undisciplined men live in this world
disguised as the disciplined.
Like a fake earring made of clay,
like a copper halfpenny covered with gold,
they live hidden in the world,
corrupt inside but beautiful outside.”
Linked Discourses 3.12
2. Childless
Five Kings
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena pañcannaṁ rājūnaṁ pasenadipamukhānaṁ pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitānaṁ samaṅgībhūtānaṁ paricārayamānānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
segs.e: Now at that time five kings headed by Pasenadi were amusing themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation, and this discussion came up among them:
“What’s the best of sensual pleasures?”
Some of them said,
“Sights are the best of sensual pleasures!”
Others said,
“Sounds are best!”
Others said,
“Smells are best!”
Others said,
“Tastes are best!”
Others said,
“Touches are best!”

segs.p: Yato kho te rājāno nāsakkhiṁsu aññamaññaṁ saññāpetuṁ.
segs.e: Since those kings were unable to persuade each other,

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo te rājāno etadavoca:
segs.e: King Pasenadi said to them,

segs.p: “āyāma, mārisā, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamissāma; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ etamatthaṁ paṭipucchissāma.
segs.e: “Come, good fellows, let’s go to the Buddha and ask him about this.

segs.p: Yathā no bhagavā byākarissati tathā naṁ dhāressāmā”ti.
segs.e: As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, mārisā”ti kho te rājāno rañño pasenadissa kosalassa paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Yes, good fellows,” replied those kings.

segs.p: Atha kho te pañca rājāno pasenadipamukhā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then those five kings headed by Pasenadi went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. King Pasenadi reported their conversation to the Buddha, and said,

segs.p: “idha, bhante, amhākaṁ pañcannaṁ rājūnaṁ pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitānaṁ samaṅgībhūtānaṁ paricārayamānānaṁ ayamantarākathā udapādi:
Kiṁ nu kho, bhante, kāmānaṁ aggan”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, what’s the best of sensual pleasures?”

segs.p: “Manāpapariyantaṁ khvāhaṁ, mahārāja, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu agganti vadāmi.
segs.e: “Great king, which kind of sensual stimulation is best is defined by which is most agreeable, I say.

segs.p: Teva, mahārāja, rūpā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva rūpā ekaccassa amanāpā honti.
segs.e: The very same sights that are agreeable to some are disagreeable to others.

segs.p: Yehi ca yo rūpehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi rūpehi aññaṁ rūpaṁ uttaritaraṁ vā paṇītataraṁ vā na pattheti.
segs.e: When you’re happy with certain sights, as you’ve got all you wished for, you don’t want any other sight that’s better or finer.
For you, those sights are perfect
and supreme.

segs.p: Teva, mahārāja, saddā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva saddā ekaccassa amanāpā honti.
segs.e: The very same sounds …

segs.p: Yehi ca yo saddehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi saddehi aññaṁ saddaṁ uttaritaraṁ vā paṇītataraṁ vā na pattheti.
Teva, mahārāja, gandhā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva gandhā ekaccassa amanāpā honti.
segs.e: smells …

segs.p: Yehi ca yo gandhehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi gandhehi aññaṁ gandhaṁ uttaritaraṁ vā paṇītataraṁ vā na pattheti.
Teva, mahārāja, rasā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva rasā ekaccassa amanāpā honti.
segs.e: tastes …

segs.p: Yehi ca yo rasehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi rasehi aññaṁ rasaṁ uttaritaraṁ vā paṇītataraṁ vā na pattheti.
Teva, mahārāja, phoṭṭhabbā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva phoṭṭhabbā ekaccassa amanāpā honti.
segs.e: touches that are agreeable to some are disagreeable to others.

segs.p: Yehi ca yo phoṭṭhabbehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi phoṭṭhabbehi aññaṁ phoṭṭhabbaṁ uttaritaraṁ vā paṇītataraṁ vā na pattheti.
segs.e: When you’re happy with certain touches, as you’ve got all you wished for, you don’t want any other touch that’s better or finer.
For you, those touches are perfect
and supreme.”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena candanaṅgaliko upāsako tassaṁ parisāyaṁ nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time the lay follower Candanaṅgalika was sitting in that assembly.

segs.p: Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then he rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said,
“I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!”
“Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako bhagavato sammukhā tadanurūpāya gāthāya abhitthavi:
segs.e: Then the lay follower Candanaṅgalika extolled the Buddha in his presence with an appropriate verse:
“Like a fragrant pink lotus
that blooms at daybreak, its fragrance unfaded—
see Aṅgīrasa dazzle,
bright as the sun in the sky!”

segs.p: Atha kho te pañca rājāno candanaṅgalikaṁ upāsakaṁ pañcahi uttarāsaṅgehi acchādesuṁ.
segs.e: Then those five kings clothed Candanaṅgalika with five upper robes.

segs.p: Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako tehi pañcahi uttarāsaṅgehi bhagavantaṁ acchādesīti.
segs.e: And Candanaṅgalika in turn endowed the Buddha with those robes.
Linked Discourses 3.13
2. Childless
A Bucketful of Rice
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo doṇapākakuraṁ bhuñjati.
segs.e: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala used to eat boiled rice by the bucketful.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhuttāvī mahassāsī yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then after eating King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, huffing and puffing. He bowed and sat down to one side.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ bhuttāviṁ mahassāsiṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, knowing that King Pasenadi was huffing and puffing after eating, on that occasion the Buddha spoke this verse:
“When a man is always mindful,
knowing moderation in eating,
his discomfort fades,
and he ages slowly, taking care of his life.”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sudassano māṇavo rañño pasenadissa kosalassa piṭṭhito ṭhito hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time the student Sudassana was standing behind the king.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo sudassanaṁ māṇavaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi addressed him,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, tāta sudassana, bhagavato santike imaṁ gāthaṁ pariyāpuṇitvā mama bhattābhihāre bhattābhihāre bhāsa.
segs.e: “Please, dear Sudassana, memorize this verse in the Buddha’s presence and recite it to me whenever I am served a meal.

segs.p: Ahañca te devasikaṁ kahāpaṇasataṁ kahāpaṇasataṁ niccaṁ bhikkhaṁ pavattayissāmī”ti.
segs.e: I’ll set up a regular daily allowance of a hundred dollars for you.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, devā”ti kho sudassano māṇavo rañño pasenadissa kosalassa paṭissutvā bhagavato santike imaṁ gāthaṁ pariyāpuṇitvā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa bhattābhihāre sudaṁ bhāsati:
segs.e: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Sudassana. He memorized that verse in the Buddha’s presence, and then whenever the king was served a meal he would repeat it:
“When a man is always mindful,
knowing moderation in eating,
his discomfort fades,
and he ages slowly, taking care of his life.”

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo anupubbena nāḷikodanaparamatāya saṇṭhāsi.
segs.e: Then the king gradually got used to having at most a cup of rice.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo aparena samayena susallikhitagatto pāṇinā gattāni anumajjanto tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ udānaṁ udānesi:
segs.e: After some time King Pasenadi’s body slimmed right down. Stroking his limbs with his hands, at that time he expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

segs.p: “ubhayena vata maṁ so bhagavā atthena anukampi—
segs.e: “In both ways the Buddha has sympathy for me:
in the good of this life and the good of lives to come.”
Linked Discourses 3.14
2. Childless
Battle (1st)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi.
segs.e: Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, mobilized an army of four divisions and marched to Kāsi to attack King Pasenadi of Kosala.
When King Pasenadi heard of this,

segs.p: “rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā mamaṁ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī”ti.
Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi.
segs.e: he mobilized an army of four divisions and marched to Kāsi to defend it against Ajātasattu.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṁ.
segs.e: Then the two kings met in battle.

segs.p: Tasmiṁ kho pana saṅgāme rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ parājesi.
segs.e: And in that battle Ajātasattu defeated Pasenadi,

segs.p: Parājito ca rājā pasenadi kosalo sakameva rājadhāniṁ sāvatthiṁ paccuyyāsi.
segs.e: who withdrew to his own capital at Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṁ piṇḍāya pavisiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

segs.p: Sāvatthiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. Then the Buddha said:

segs.p: “Idha, bhante, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi.
Assosi kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo:
‘rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā mamaṁ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī’ti.
Atha kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi.
Atha kho, bhante, rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṁ.
Tasmiṁ kho pana, bhante, saṅgāme rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ parājesi.
Parājito ca, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo sakameva rājadhāniṁ sāvatthiṁ paccuyyāsī”ti.
“Rājā, bhikkhave, māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto pāpamitto pāpasahāyo pāpasampavaṅko;
segs.e: “Mendicants, King Ajātasattu has bad friends, companions, and associates.

segs.p: rājā ca kho, bhikkhave, pasenadi kosalo kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko.
segs.e: But King Pasenadi has good friends, companions, and associates.

segs.p: Ajjeva, bhikkhave, rājā pasenadi kosalo imaṁ rattiṁ dukkhaṁ seti parājito”ti.
segs.e: Yet on this day King Pasenadi will have a bad night’s sleep as one defeated.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“Victory breeds enmity;
the defeated sleep badly.
The peaceful sleep at ease,
having left victory and defeat behind.”
Linked Discourses 3.15
2. Childless
Battle (2nd)

segs.p: Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi.
segs.e: Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, mobilized an army of four divisions and marched to Kāsi to attack King Pasenadi of Kosala.
When King Pasenadi heard of this,

segs.p: “rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā mamaṁ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī”ti.
Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi.
segs.e: he mobilized an army of four divisions and marched to Kāsi to defend it against Ajātasattu.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṁ.
segs.e: Then the two kings met in battle.

segs.p: Tasmiṁ kho pana saṅgāme rājā pasenadi kosalo rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ parājesi, jīvaggāhañca naṁ aggahesi.
segs.e: And in that battle Pasenadi defeated Ajātasattu and captured him alive.

segs.p: Atha kho rañño pasenadissa kosalassa etadahosi:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi thought,

segs.p: “kiñcāpi kho myāyaṁ rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto adubbhantassa dubbhati, atha ca pana me bhāgineyyo hoti.
segs.e: “Even though I’ve never betrayed this King Ajātasattu, he betrayed me. Still, he is my nephew.

segs.p: Yannūnāhaṁ rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṁ hatthikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ assakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ rathakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ pattikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṁ osajjeyyan”ti.
segs.e: Now that I’ve vanquished all of Ajātasattu’s elephant troops, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, why don’t I let him loose with just his life?”

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṁ hatthikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ assakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ rathakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ pattikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṁ osajji.
segs.e: And that’s what he did.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṁ piṇḍāya pavisiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants …

segs.p: Sāvatthiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: told the Buddha what had happened.

segs.p: “Idha, bhante, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi.
Assosi kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo:
‘rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā mamaṁ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī’ti.
Atha kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṁ senaṁ sannayhitvā rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi.
Atha kho, bhante, rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṁ.
Tasmiṁ kho pana, bhante, saṅgāme rājā pasenadi kosalo rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ ajātasattuṁ vedehiputtaṁ parājesi, jīvaggāhañca naṁ aggahesi.
Atha kho, bhante, rañño pasenadissa kosalassa etadahosi:
‘kiñcāpi kho myāyaṁ rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto adubbhantassa dubbhati, atha ca pana me bhāgineyyo hoti.
Yannūnāhaṁ rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṁ hatthikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ assakāyaṁ sabbaṁ rathakāyaṁ sabbaṁ pattikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṁ osajjeyyan’”ti.

“Atha kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṁ hatthikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ assakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ rathakāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṁ pattikāyaṁ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṁ osajjī”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:
“A man goes on plundering
as long as it serves his ends.
But as soon as others plunder him,
the plunderer is plundered.
For the fool thinks they’re on solid ground,
so long as their wickedness has not ripened.
But as soon as that wickedness ripens,
they fall into suffering.
A killer creates a killer;
a conqueror creates a conqueror;
an abuser creates abuse,
and a bully creates a bully.
And so as deeds unfold
the plunderer is plundered.”
Linked Discourses 3.16
2. Childless
A Daughter
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro puriso yena rājā pasenadi kosalo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa upakaṇṇake ārocesi:
segs.e: Then a man went up to the king and whispered in his ear,
“Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has given birth to a daughter.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, rājā pasenadi kosalo anattamano ahosi.
segs.e: When this was said, King Pasenadi was disappointed.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ anattamanataṁ viditvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then, knowing that King Pasenadi was disappointed, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:
“Well, some women are better than men,
O ruler of the people.
Wise and virtuous, a devoted wife
whose mother-in-law is her queen.
And when she has a son,
he becomes a hero, O lord of the land.
The son of such a blessed lady
may even rule the realm.”
Linked Discourses 3.17
2. Childless
Diligence
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “atthi nu kho, bhante, eko dhammo yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati—
segs.e: “Sir, is there one thing that secures benefits for both
this life and lives to come?”

segs.p: “Atthi kho, mahārāja, eko dhammo yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati—
segs.e: “There is, Great King.”

segs.p: “Katamo pana, bhante, eko dhammo, yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati—
segs.e: “So what is that one thing?”

segs.p: “Appamādo kho, mahārāja, eko dhammo, yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati—
segs.e: “Diligence, Great King, is one thing that secures benefits for both
this life and lives to come.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, yāni kānici jaṅgalānaṁ pāṇānaṁ padajātāni, sabbāni tāni hatthipade samodhānaṁ gacchanti, hatthipadaṁ tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati—yadidaṁ mahantattena;
segs.e: The footprints of all creatures that walk can fit inside an elephant’s footprint. So an elephant’s footprint is said to be the biggest of them all.

segs.p: evameva kho, mahārāja, appamādo eko dhammo, yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati—
segs.e: In the same way, diligence is one thing that secures benefits for both
this life and lives to come.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“For one who desires high delights
again and again—
long life, beauty, and health,
heaven, and an eminent family—
the astute praise diligence
in making merit.
Being diligent, an astute person
secures both benefits:
the benefit in this life,
and in lives to come.
An attentive one, comprehending the meaning,
is said to be astute.”
Linked Discourses 3.18
2. Childless
Good Friends
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

segs.p: ‘svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, so ca kho kalyāṇamittassa kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa, no pāpamittassa no pāpasahāyassa no pāpasampavaṅkassā’”ti.
segs.e: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha. But it’s for someone with good friends, companions, and associates, not for someone with bad friends, companions, and associates.’”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

segs.p: Svākkhāto, mahārāja, mayā dhammo. So ca kho kalyāṇamittassa kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa, no pāpamittassa no pāpasahāyassa no pāpasampavaṅkassāti.
Ekamidāhaṁ, mahārāja, samayaṁ sakkesu viharāmi nagarakaṁ nāma sakyānaṁ nigamo.
segs.e: “Great king, this one time I was staying in the land of the Sakyans where they have a town named Townsville.

segs.p: Atha kho, mahārāja, ānando bhikkhu yenāhaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā maṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho, mahārāja, ānando bhikkhu maṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the mendicant Ānanda came to me, bowed, sat down to one side, and said:
‘Sir, good friends, companions, and associates are half the spiritual life.’

segs.p: Evaṁ vuttāhaṁ, mahārāja, ānandaṁ bhikkhuṁ etadavocaṁ:
segs.e: When he had spoken, I said to him:
‘Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!

segs.p: Sakalameva hidaṁ, ānanda, brahmacariyaṁ—yadidaṁ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā.
segs.e: Good friends, companions, and associates are the whole of the spiritual life.

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassetaṁ, ānanda, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṁ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bhāvessati ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bahulīkarissati.
segs.e: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path.

segs.p: Kathañca, ānanda, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bhāveti, ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bahulīkaroti?
segs.e: And how does a mendicant with good friends develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṁ bhāveti vivekanissitaṁ virāganissitaṁ nirodhanissitaṁ vossaggapariṇāmiṁ, sammāsaṅkappaṁ bhāveti … sammāvācaṁ bhāveti … sammākammantaṁ bhāveti … sammāājīvaṁ bhāveti … sammāvāyāmaṁ bhāveti … sammāsatiṁ bhāveti … sammāsamādhiṁ bhāveti vivekanissitaṁ virāganissitaṁ nirodhanissitaṁ vossaggapariṇāmiṁ.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant develops right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, ānanda, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bhāveti, ariyaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ bahulīkaroti.
segs.e: That’s how a mendicant with good friends develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path.

segs.p: Tadamināpetaṁ, ānanda, pariyāyena veditabbaṁ yathā sakalamevidaṁ brahmacariyaṁ—yadidaṁ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatāti.
segs.e: And here’s another way to understand how good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.

segs.p: Mamañhi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṁ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccanti, jarādhammā sattā jarāya parimuccanti, byādhidhammā sattā byādhito parimuccanti, maraṇadhammā sattā maraṇena parimuccanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā sattā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsehi parimuccanti.
segs.e: For, by relying on me as a good friend, sentient beings who are liable to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are freed from all these things.

segs.p: Iminā kho etaṁ, ānanda, pariyāyena veditabbaṁ yathā sakalamevidaṁ brahmacariyaṁ—yadidaṁ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā’ti.
segs.e: This is another way to understand how good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.’
So, Great King, you should train like this:
‘I will have good friends, companions, and associates.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: Kalyāṇamittassa te, mahārāja, kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa ayaṁ eko dhammo upanissāya vihātabbo—
segs.e: When you have good friends, companions, and associates, you should live supported by one thing:
diligence in skillful qualities.

segs.p: Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṁ upanissāya, itthāgārassa anuyantassa evaṁ bhavissati:
segs.e: When you’re diligent, supported by diligence, your ladies of the harem,

segs.p: Handa mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṁ upanissāyā’ti.
Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṁ upanissāya, khattiyānampi anuyantānaṁ evaṁ bhavissati:
segs.e: aristocrat vassals,

segs.p: Handa mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṁ upanissāyā’ti.
Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṁ upanissāya, balakāyassapi evaṁ bhavissati:
segs.e: troops,

segs.p: Handa mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṁ upanissāyā’ti.
Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṁ upanissāya, negamajānapadassapi evaṁ bhavissati:
segs.e: and people of town and country will think:
‘The king lives diligently, supported by diligence.

segs.p: Handa mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṁ upanissāyā’ti?
segs.e: We’d better live diligently, supported by diligence!’

segs.p: Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṁ upanissāya, attāpi gutto rakkhito bhavissati—
segs.e: When you’re diligent, supported by diligence, then not only you yourself,

segs.p: itthāgārampi guttaṁ rakkhitaṁ bhavissati, kosakoṭṭhāgārampi guttaṁ rakkhitaṁ bhavissatī”ti.
segs.e: but your ladies of the harem, and your treasury and storehouses will be guarded and protected.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“For one who desires high wealth
again and again,
the astute praise diligence
in making merit.
Being diligent, an astute person
secures both benefits:
the benefit in this life,
and in lives to come.
Attentive, comprehending the meaning,
they are said to be astute.”
Linked Discourses 3.19
2. Childless
Childless (1st)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo divā divassa yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha in the middle of the day, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “handa kuto nu tvaṁ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti?
segs.e: “So, Great King, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”
“Sir, here in Sāvatthī a financier householder has passed away.

segs.p: Tamahaṁ aputtakaṁ sāpateyyaṁ rājantepuraṁ atiharitvā āgacchāmi.
segs.e: Since he died childless, I have come after transferring his fortune to the royal compound.

segs.p: Asīti, bhante, satasahassāni hiraññasseva, ko pana vādo rūpiyassa.
segs.e: There was eight million in gold coin, not to mention the silver coin.

segs.p: Tassa kho pana, bhante, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa evarūpo bhattabhogo ahosi—
segs.e: And yet that financier ate meals of
sour gruel with false black pepper.
He wore clothes consisting of
three patches of sunn hemp.
He traveled around in a vehicle that was
a dilapidated little cart, holding a leaf as parasol.”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!

segs.p: Asappuriso kho, mahārāja, uḷāre bhoge labhitvā nevattānaṁ sukheti pīṇeti, na mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, na puttadāraṁ sukheti pīṇeti, na dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, na mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, na samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṁ sukhavipākaṁ saggasaṁvattanikaṁ.
segs.e: When an untrue person has acquired notable wealth they don’t make themselves happy and pleased. Nor do they make their mother and father, partners and children, bondservants, workers, and staff, and friends and colleagues happy and pleased. And they don’t establish an uplifting religious donation for ascetics and brahmins that’s conducive to heaven, ripens in happiness, and leads to heaven.

segs.p: Tassa te bhoge evaṁ sammā aparibhuñjiyamāne rājāno vā haranti corā vā haranti aggi vā ḍahati udakaṁ vā vahati appiyā vā dāyādā haranti.
segs.e: Because they haven’t made proper use of that wealth, rulers or bandits take it, or fire consumes it, or flood sweeps it away, or unloved heirs take it.

segs.p: Evaṁsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā aparibhuñjiyamānā parikkhayaṁ gacchanti, no paribhogaṁ.
segs.e: Since that wealth is not properly utilized, it’s wasted, not used.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, amanussaṭṭhāne pokkharaṇī acchodakā sītodakā sātodakā setodakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā.
segs.e: Suppose there was a lotus pond in an uninhabited region with clear, sweet, cool water, clean, with smooth banks, delightful.

segs.p: Taṁ jano neva hareyya na piveyya na nahāyeyya na yathāpaccayaṁ vā kareyya.
segs.e: But people don’t collect it or drink it or bathe in it or use it for any purpose.

segs.p: Evañhi taṁ, mahārāja, udakaṁ sammā aparibhuñjiyamānaṁ parikkhayaṁ gaccheyya, no paribhogaṁ.
segs.e: Since that water is not properly utilized, it’s wasted, not used.

segs.p: Evameva kho, mahārāja, asappuriso uḷāre bhoge labhitvā nevattānaṁ sukheti pīṇeti, na mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, na puttadāraṁ sukheti pīṇeti, na dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, na mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, na samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṁ sukhavipākaṁ saggasaṁvattanikaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, when an untrue person has acquired notable wealth …

segs.p: Tassa te bhoge evaṁ sammā aparibhuñjiyamāne rājāno vā haranti, corā vā haranti, aggi vā ḍahati, udakaṁ vā vahati, appiyā vā dāyādā haranti.
Evaṁsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā aparibhuñjiyamānā parikkhayaṁ gacchanti, no paribhogaṁ.
segs.e: it’s wasted, not used.

segs.p: Sappuriso ca kho, mahārāja, uḷāre bhoge labhitvā attānaṁ sukheti pīṇeti, mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, puttadāraṁ sukheti pīṇeti, dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṁ sukhavipākaṁ saggasaṁvattanikaṁ.
segs.e: When a true person has acquired notable wealth they make themselves happy and pleased. And they make their mother and father, partners and children, bondservants, workers, and staff, and friends and colleagues happy and pleased. And they establish an uplifting religious donation for ascetics and brahmins that’s conducive to heaven, ripens in happiness, and leads to heaven.

segs.p: Tassa te bhoge evaṁ sammā paribhuñjiyamāne neva rājāno haranti, na corā haranti, na aggi ḍahati, na udakaṁ vahati, na appiyā dāyādā haranti.
segs.e: Because they make proper use of that wealth, rulers or bandits don’t take it, fire doesn’t consume it, flood doesn’t sweep it away, and unloved heirs don’t take it.

segs.p: Evaṁsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā paribhuñjiyamānā paribhogaṁ gacchanti, no parikkhayaṁ.
segs.e: Since that wealth is properly utilized, it’s used, not wasted.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre pokkharaṇī acchodakā sītodakā sātodakā setodakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā.
segs.e: Suppose there was a lotus pond not far from a town or village with clear, sweet, cool water, clean, with smooth banks, delightful.

segs.p: Tañca udakaṁ jano hareyyapi piveyyapi nahāyeyyapi yathāpaccayampi kareyya.
segs.e: And people collected it and drank it and bathed in it and used it for their own purpose.

segs.p: Evañhi taṁ, mahārāja, udakaṁ sammā paribhuñjiyamānaṁ paribhogaṁ gaccheyya, no parikkhayaṁ.
segs.e: Since that water is properly utilized, it’s used, not wasted.

segs.p: Evameva kho, mahārāja, sappuriso uḷāre bhoge labhitvā attānaṁ sukheti pīṇeti, mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, puttadāraṁ sukheti pīṇeti, dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṁ sukhavipākaṁ saggasaṁvattanikaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, when a true person has acquired notable wealth …

segs.p: Tassa te bhoge evaṁ sammā paribhuñjiyamāne neva rājāno haranti, na corā haranti, na aggi ḍahati, na udakaṁ vahati, na appiyā dāyādā haranti.
Evaṁsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā paribhuñjiyamānā paribhogaṁ gacchanti, no parikkhayan”ti.
segs.e: it’s used, not wasted.
As cool water in an uninhabited region
evaporates when not drunk;
so too when a reprobate acquires wealth,
they neither use it themselves nor give it away.
When the attentive and sensible acquire wealth,
they use it, being dutiful.
That boss, having supported the family unit,
blameless, goes to a heavenly place.”

2. Childless
Childless (2nd)

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo divā divassa yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha in the middle of the day … The Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “handa kuto nu tvaṁ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti?
segs.e: “So, Great King, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”
“Sir, here in Sāvatthī a financier householder has passed away.

segs.p: Tamahaṁ aputtakaṁ sāpateyyaṁ rājantepuraṁ atiharitvā āgacchāmi.
segs.e: Since he died childless, I have come after transferring his fortune to the royal compound.

segs.p: Sataṁ, bhante, satasahassāni hiraññasseva, ko pana vādo rūpiyassa.
segs.e: There was ten million in gold coin, not to mention the silver coin.

segs.p: Tassa kho pana, bhante, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa evarūpo bhattabhogo ahosi—
segs.e: And yet that financier ate meals of
sour gruel with false black pepper.
He wore clothes consisting of
three patches of sunn hemp.
He traveled around in a vehicle that was
a dilapidated little cart, holding a leaf as parasol.”
“That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati taggarasikhiṁ nāma paccekasambuddhaṁ piṇḍapātena paṭipādesi.
segs.e: Once upon a time, great king, that financier householder provided almsfood on behalf of an independent Buddha named Tagarasikhī.
He instructed: ‘Give alms to that ascetic,’ before getting up from his seat and leaving.

segs.p: Datvā ca pana pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi:
segs.e: But after giving he regretted it:

segs.p: ‘varametaṁ piṇḍapātaṁ dāsā vā kammakarā vā bhuñjeyyun’ti.
segs.e: ‘It would have been better to feed the bondservants or workers with that almsfood.’

segs.p: Bhātu ca pana ekaputtakaṁ sāpateyyassa kāraṇā jīvitā voropesi.
segs.e: What’s more, he murdered his brother’s only child for the sake of his fortune.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati taggarasikhiṁ paccekasambuddhaṁ piṇḍapātena paṭipādesi, tassa kammassa vipākena sattakkhattuṁ sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajji.
segs.e: Because that financier provided Tagarasikhī with almsfood, as a result of that deed he was reborn seven times in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena imissāyeva sāvatthiyā sattakkhattuṁ seṭṭhittaṁ kāresi.
segs.e: And as a residual result of that same deed he held the position of financier seven times right here in Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati datvā pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi:
segs.e: But because that financier regretted giving alms,

segs.p: ‘varametaṁ piṇḍapātaṁ dāsā vā kammakarā vā bhuñjeyyun’ti, tassa kammassa vipākena nāssuḷārāya bhattabhogāya cittaṁ namati, nāssuḷārāya vatthabhogāya cittaṁ namati, nāssuḷārāya yānabhogāya cittaṁ namati, nāssuḷārānaṁ pañcannaṁ kāmaguṇānaṁ bhogāya cittaṁ namati.
segs.e: as a result of that deed his mind didn’t tend to enjoy nice food, clothes, vehicles, or the five refined kinds of sensual stimulation.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati bhātu ca pana ekaputtakaṁ sāpateyyassa kāraṇā jīvitā voropesi, tassa kammassa vipākena bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni bahūni vassasahassāni bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccittha.
segs.e: And because that financier murdered his brother’s only child for the sake of his fortune, as a result of that deed he burned in hell for many years, for many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of years.

segs.p: Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena idaṁ sattamaṁ aputtakaṁ sāpateyyaṁ rājakosaṁ paveseti.
segs.e: And as a residual result of that same deed, he is childless for the seventh time, his fortune ending up in the royal treasury.

segs.p: Tassa kho, mahārāja, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa purāṇañca puññaṁ parikkhīṇaṁ, navañca puññaṁ anupacitaṁ.
segs.e: Now the old merit of that financier has been used up, and he hasn’t accumulated new merit.

segs.p: Ajja pana, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruve niraye paccatī”ti.
segs.e: Today, Great King, that financier burns in the Great Hell of Screams.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruvaṁ nirayaṁ upapanno”ti.
segs.e: “Really, sir, that financier has been reborn in the Great Hell of Screams?”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruvaṁ nirayaṁ upapanno”ti.
segs.e: “Yes he has, Great King.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“Grain, money, silver, and gold,
or whatever other possessions there are;
bondservants, workers, servants,
and those dependent for their livelihood:
you must go on without taking these;
all of them are left behind.
But the deeds you do
by body, speech, and mind—
that’s what you can call your own.
That’s what you take when you go.
That’s what goes with you,
like a shadow that never leaves.
That’s why you should do good,
investing in the future life.
The good deeds of sentient beings
support them in the next world.”

3. Kosala
Individuals
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:
“Great king, these four individuals are found in the world.
What four?
The dark bound for darkness,
the dark bound for light,
the light bound for darkness,
and the light bound for light.
And how is an individual dark and bound for darkness?

segs.p: Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo nīce kule paccājāto hoti, caṇḍālakule vā venakule vā nesādakule vā rathakārakule vā pukkusakule vā dalidde appannapānabhojane kasiravuttike, yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhati.
segs.e: It’s when an individual is reborn in a low family—a family of corpse-workers, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or scavengers—poor, with little to eat or drink, where life is tough, and food and shelter are hard to find.

segs.p: So ca hoti dubbaṇṇo duddasiko okoṭimako bavhābādho kāṇo vā kuṇī vā khañjo vā pakkhahato vā, na lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa.
segs.e: And they’re ugly, unsightly, deformed, sickly—one-eyed, crippled, lame, or half-paralyzed. They don’t get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; or bed, house, and lighting.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: And they do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ caritvā vācāya duccaritaṁ caritvā manasā duccaritaṁ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso andhakārā vā andhakāraṁ gaccheyya, tamā vā tamaṁ gaccheyya, lohitamalā vā lohitamalaṁ gaccheyya.
segs.e: This individual is like someone who goes from darkness to darkness, from blackness to blackness, from bloodstain to bloodstain.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, mahārāja, puggalo tamotamaparāyano hoti.
segs.e: That’s how an individual is dark and bound for darkness.
And how is an individual dark and bound for light?

segs.p: Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo nīce kule paccājāto hoti, caṇḍālakule vā venakule vā nesādakule vā rathakārakule vā pukkusakule vā dalidde appannapānabhojane kasiravuttike, yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhati.
segs.e: It’s when an individual is reborn in a low family—a family of corpse-workers, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or scavengers—poor, with little to eat or drink, where life is tough, and food and shelter are hard to find.

segs.p: So ca kho hoti dubbaṇṇo duddasiko okoṭimako bavhābādho, kāṇo vā kuṇī vā khañjo vā pakkhahato vā, na lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa.
segs.e: And they’re ugly, unsightly, deformed, sickly—one-eyed, crippled, lame, or half-paralyzed. They don’t get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; or bed, house, and lighting.

segs.p: So kāyena sucaritaṁ carati, vācāya sucaritaṁ carati, manasā sucaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: But they do good things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena sucaritaṁ caritvā vācāya sucaritaṁ caritvā manasā sucaritaṁ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pathaviyā vā pallaṅkaṁ āroheyya, pallaṅkā vā assapiṭṭhiṁ āroheyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā hatthikkhandhaṁ āroheyya, hatthikkhandhā vā pāsādaṁ āroheyya.
segs.e: This individual is like someone who ascends from the ground to a couch; from a couch to horseback; from horseback to an elephant; and from an elephant to a stilt longhouse.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, mahārāja, puggalo tamojotiparāyano hoti.
segs.e: That’s how an individual is dark and bound for light.
And how is an individual light and bound for darkness?

segs.p: Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo ucce kule paccājāto hoti, khattiyamahāsālakule vā brāhmaṇamahāsālakule vā gahapatimahāsālakule vā, aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate pahūtavittūpakaraṇe pahūtadhanadhaññe.
segs.e: It’s when an individual is reborn in an eminent family—a well-to-do family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain.

segs.p: So ca hoti abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko, paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato, lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa.
segs.e: And they’re attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. They get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: But they do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ caritvā vācāya duccaritaṁ caritvā manasā duccaritaṁ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pāsādā vā hatthikkhandhaṁ oroheyya, hatthikkhandhā vā assapiṭṭhiṁ oroheyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā pallaṅkaṁ oroheyya, pallaṅkā vā pathaviṁ oroheyya, pathaviyā vā andhakāraṁ paviseyya.
segs.e: This individual is like someone who descends from a stilt longhouse to an elephant; from an elephant to horseback; from horseback to a couch; and from a couch to the ground; and from the ground they enter darkness.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, mahārāja, puggalo jotitamaparāyano hoti.
segs.e: That’s how an individual is light and bound for darkness.
And how is an individual light and bound for light?

segs.p: Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo ucce kule paccājāto hoti, khattiyamahāsālakule vā brāhmaṇamahāsālakule vā gahapatimahāsālakule vā, aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate pahūtavittūpakaraṇe pahūtadhanadhaññe.
segs.e: It’s when an individual is reborn in an eminent family—a well-to-do family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain.

segs.p: So ca hoti abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko, paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato, lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa.
segs.e: And they’re attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. They get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting.

segs.p: So kāyena sucaritaṁ carati, vācāya sucaritaṁ carati, manasā sucaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: And they do good things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena sucaritaṁ caritvā vācāya sucaritaṁ caritvā manasā sucaritaṁ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pallaṅkā vā pallaṅkaṁ saṅkameyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā assapiṭṭhiṁ saṅkameyya, hatthikkhandhā vā hatthikkhandhaṁ saṅkameyya, pāsādā vā pāsādaṁ saṅkameyya.
segs.e: This individual is like someone who shifts from one couch to another; from the back of one horse to another; from one elephant to another; or from one stilt longhouse to another.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, mahārāja, puggalo jotijotiparāyano hoti.
segs.e: That’s how an individual is light and bound for light.

segs.p: Ime kho, mahārāja, cattāro puggalā santo saṁvijjamānā lokasmin”ti.
segs.e: These are the four individuals found in the world.”
That is what the Buddha said. …
“O King, some people are poor,
faithless and stingy.
Miserly, with bad intentions,
they lack regard, they have wrong view.
They abuse and insult
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants.
They’re nihilists and bullies,
who prevent others from giving
food to beggars.
O King, ruler of the people:
when such people die
they fall into the terrible hell—
from darkness they’re bound for darkness.
O King, some people are poor,
but faithful and not stingy.
They give with best of intentions,
that peaceful-hearted person.
They rise for and bow to
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants.
Training in moral conduct,
they don’t prevent others from giving
food to beggars.
O King, ruler of the people:
when such people die
they go to the Third Heaven—
from darkness they’re bound for light.
O King, some people are rich,
but faithless and stingy.
Miserly, with bad intentions,
they lack regard, they have wrong view.
They abuse and insult
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants
They’re nihilists and bullies,
who prevent others from giving
food to beggars.
O King, ruler of the people:
when such people die
they fall into the terrible hell—
from light they’re bound for darkness.
O King, some people are rich,
faithful and not stingy.
They give with best of intentions,
that peaceful-hearted person.
They rise for and bow to
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants.
Training in moral conduct,
they don’t prevent others from giving
food to beggars.
O King, ruler of the people:
when such people die
they go to the Third Heaven—
from light they’re bound for light.”
